words: مَا سَمِعْنَا بِهَٰذَا فِى ٱلْمِلَّةِ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an cannot have been altered or lost: God guaranteed its preservation, and the multitudes who memorized it across places and circumstances would have exposed any change.
rows.anchor: وقد ضمن الله حفظ كتابه أن يأتيه الباطل من بين يديه أو من خلفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's many distinct audiences memorized it for recitation, law, interpretation, eloquence, or scrutiny, making coordinated concealment or alteration implausible.
rows.anchor: وكيف يجوز على أهل هذه الهمم المختلفة والآراء المتباينة - على كثرة أعدادهم واختلاف بلادهم وتفاوت أغراضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even a single changed word in Imruʾ al-Qays would have been disowned despite poetry's lesser importance; alteration of the Qur'an, essential to prayer and law, is still less conceivable.
rows.anchor: لو زيد فيه بيت أو نقص منه بيت لا بل لو غير فيه لفظ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some opponents dismissed the revelation as fabricated, claiming they had not heard such a thing in the latest religion.
rows.anchor: قول بعضهم ( ﴿ ما سمعنا بهذا في الملة الآخرة إن هذا إلا اختلاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports about earlier unseen events are evidence for Muhammad's prophethood; the Qur'an stresses that he had not learned these events from prior scripture or witnesses.
rows.anchor: فبين وجه دلالته من إخباره بهذه الأمور الغائبة السالفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To establish that the Qur'an's order exceeds familiar styles, Bāqillānī says one must show that it is not poetry, sajʿ, or metrical speech.
rows.anchor: ومن ادعى ذلك لم يكن له بد من أن يصحح أنه ليس من قبيل الشعر ولا السجع ولا الكلام الموزون

rows.speaker: كفار قريش
rows.claim: Some Quraysh disbelievers classified the Qur'an as poetry.
rows.anchor: لأن قوما من كفار قريش ادعوا أنه شعر

rows.speaker: الملحدة
rows.claim: Some heretics claimed that the Qur'an contains poetry.
rows.anchor: ومن الملحدة من يزعم أن فيه شعرا

rows.speaker: أهل الملة
rows.claim: Some Muslims described the Qur'an as rhymed prose, though more eloquent than the sajʿ they knew.
rows.anchor: ومن أهل الملة من يقول إنه كلام مسجع إلا أنه أفصح مما قد اعتادوه من أسجاعهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others claimed the Qur'an was metrical speech, which would still place it within familiar forms of discourse.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من يدعى أنه كلام موزون

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some authorities said the first revelation was 'Read in the name of your Lord.'
rows.anchor: فمنهم من قال قوله ( ﴿ اقرأ باسم ربك ﴾ )

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others said the first revelation was 'O you wrapped up.'
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال ( ﴿ يا أيها المدثر ﴾ )

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further view named the Opening of the Book as the first revelation.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال فاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identified Sūrat al-Naṣr as the last revelation.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس ( ﴿ إذا جاء نصر الله ﴾

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha identified Sūrat al-Māʾida as the last revelation.
rows.anchor: وقالت عائشة سورة المائدة

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib identified Sūrat Barāʾa as the last revelation.
rows.anchor: وقال البراء بن عازب آخر ما أنزل سورة براءة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr identified the verse about the day people return to God as the last revelation.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير آخر ما أنزل قوله تعالى ( ﴿ واتقوا يوما ترجعون فيه إلى الله ﴾

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identified the instruction to say 'God is sufficient for me' as the last revelation.
rows.anchor: وقال السدى آخر ما أنزل ( ﴿ فإن تولوا فقل حسبي الله لا إله إلا هو عليه توكلت ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports can differ because each authority may have named the last passage he personally heard; disagreement over its placement is not disagreement over the Qur'an's source.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون في مثل هذا خلاف وأن يكون كل واحد ذكر آخر ما سمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's style differs from the Prophet's ordinary speech as sharply as one man's sermon differs from another; its order is outside familiar speech patterns.
rows.anchor: لكان البون بين كلامه وبينه مثل ما بين خطبة وخطبة ينشئهما رجل واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recognizing distinctions among poetic and other speech forms requires reflection and acquired discernment, not automatic perception.
rows.anchor: ويحتاج في معرفة ذوق الشعر ووزنه والفرق بينه وبين غيره من الأوزان يحتاج إلى نظر وتأمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proof remains valid even when believers disagree about how it demonstrates its conclusion, just as they differ over arguments for the world's origination.
rows.anchor: قد يثبت الشيء دليلا وإن اختلفوا في وجه دلالة البرهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's composition lies outside familiar Arabic genres: poetry, unrhymed meter, sajʿ, mixed forms, and ordinary prose; it has a distinctive style throughout.
rows.anchor: وقد علمنا أن القرآن خارج عن هذه الوجوه ومباين لهذه الطرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No Arab author produced a work of comparable length with the Qur'an's eloquence, rare expression, inventive range, subtle meanings, abundant wisdom, and rhetorical harmony.
rows.anchor: ليس للعرب كلام مشتمل على هذه الفصاحة والغرابة والتصرف البديع والمعاني اللطيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an remains harmonious across its length; extended human speech develops variation and flaws, as the Qur'an itself says of speech from other than God.
rows.anchor: وقد حصل القران على كثرته وطوله متناسبا في الفصاحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's distinctive evidence extends from individual words and phrases through complete stories, chapters, and the whole book, though some passages show it more clearly.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت الدلالة في البعض أبين وأظهر والآية أكشف وأبهر

words: تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Contemplating the Qur'an can illuminate and convince the mind while producing awe, emotional trembling, joy, and a heightened sense of certainty.
rows.anchor: الرعب يأخذ منك مأخذه

words: ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's influence is visible in public life and hearts, and its required preservation and recitation in prayer demonstrate its great rank; it is opened with the commanded refuge prayer.
rows.anchor: جعل عماد الصلاة التي هي تلو الإيمان في التأكيد وثانيه التوحيد في الوجوب

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī said that masters of poetry are fewer than masters of war.
rows.anchor: سمعت الأصمعي يقول فرسان الشعر أقل من فرسان الحرب

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said that scholars of poetry are rarer than red sulfur.
rows.anchor: وقال سمعت أبا عمرو بن العلاء يقول العلماء بالشعر أعز من الكبريت الأحمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary speech is difficult to judge and critics often disagree about its merits; the most eloquent Arabs were bewildered by the Qur'an and answered with conjecture and dismissive labels.
rows.anchor: وقد حير القوم الذين لم يكن أحد أفصح منهم ولا أتم بلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's description of the Qur'an as the best speech suffices to establish its excellence; a small sample can disclose the quality of a larger work.
rows.anchor: فليس يوقف على حسن الكلام بطوله ولا تعرف براعته بكثرة فصوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God's guidance enables recognition of the Qur'an's excellence; God guides or misguides many through it.
rows.anchor: فلا تعلم ما وصفنا لك إلا بهداية من العزيز الحميد

rows.speaker: خطيب غير مسمى
rows.claim: The sermon calls God's book the best and most eloquent speech and praises those whom God adorns with it and brings to Islam.
rows.anchor: إن أحسن الحديث كتاب الله قد أفلح من زينه الله في قلبه

rows.speaker: خطيب غير مسمى
rows.claim: The sermon urges love of God and those He loves, continued attention to God's speech and remembrance, worship without associating partners, and mutual love through God's spirit.
rows.anchor: ولا تملوا كلام الله وذكره ولا تقسو عليه قلوبكم اعبدوا الله ولا تشركوا به شيئا

words: فَمَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُم مَّا كَانُوا۟ يَكْسِبُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A compact passage relates the story's meaning in only a few verses while yielding many lessons that would otherwise require lengthy explanation.
rows.anchor: في ثلاث آيات بعد ذلك معنى هذه القصة التي كانت لهم بكلمات قليلة في العدد كثيرة الفوائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning moves gradually into the reminder that good and evil actions return to their doer, then into hope of mercy; these transitions preserve the discourse's order.
rows.anchor: ثم لم يخل تضاعيف الكلام مما ترى من الموعظة على أعجب تدريج وأبدع تأريخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse stays connected while shifting topics, so inserting unrelated material would disrupt its seamless order; its exploration keeps yielding further benefits and wisdom.
rows.anchor: ولم ينقطع بذلك نظام الكلام وأنت ترى الكلام يتبدد مع اتصاله وينتشر مع انتظامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāqillānī calls those who compare the Qur'an with Imruʾ al-Qays's poetry profoundly foolish, arguing that the poet's work contains obscure, coarse, and inept lines.
rows.anchor: إن الذي عارض القرآن بشعر امرئ القيس لأضل من حمار باهلة وأحمق من هبنقة

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī admitted he could not identify the meanings of the words san, sannaq, and sanam; another gloss took sannaq to mean a hill.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي لا أدري ما السن ولا السنيق ولا السنم وقال بعضهم السنيق أكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's descent through the Trustworthy Spirit to Muhammad in clear Arabic makes him a warner and establishes the Qur'an's language as a proof.
rows.anchor: فلولا أن كونه بهذا اللسان حجة لم يعقب كلامه الأول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many sūras opened by disconnected letters are structured from beginning to end to establish the Qur'an's compelling proof and inimitability.
rows.anchor: وكثير من هذه السور إذا تأملته فهو من أوله إلى آخره مبني على لزوم حجة القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Sūrat al-Muʾmin, disputing God's signs is called disbelief; the account of earlier peoples' rejection and punishment supports this warning.
rows.anchor: فدل على أن الجدال في تنزيله كفر وإلحاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' prayer for believers shows that accepting the Qur'an's conclusive proof is praiseworthy, just as rejecting it deserves blame.
rows.anchor: فلولا أنه برهان قاهر لم يذم الكفار على العدول عنه ولم يحمد المؤمنين على المصير إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāqillānī judges the sexual boast in Imruʾ al-Qays's first quoted line obscene, pointless, repellent to listeners, and lacking either fine expression or good meaning.
rows.anchor: فالبيت الأول غاية في الفحش ونهاية في السخف وأي فائدة لذكره لعشيقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next line about a beloved's refusal is badly woven and offers no useful reason to report that she resisted him at a named place.
rows.anchor: فهو كلام رديء النسج لا فائدة لذكره لنا أن حبيبته تمنعت عليه يوما بموضع يسميه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He finds the line addressed to Fāṭima limp and effeminate; the defense that feminine verse suits women's nature fails because poets retain firmness in feminine poetry.
rows.anchor: فالبيت الأول فيه ركاكة جدا وتأنيث ورقة ولكن فيها تخنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second hemistich does not fit the first or its preceding verse, and scolding a beloved for coyness conflicts with the lover's delight in it.
rows.anchor: والمصراع الثاني منقطع عن الأول لا يلائمه ولا يوافقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line claiming that the beloved's commands govern the speaker's heart is criticized as inconsistent with his earlier displays of love and weeping, unless it shifts to an incompatible pose of toughness.
rows.anchor: فهذا خلاف ما أظهر من نفسه فيما تقدم من الأبيات من الحب والبكاء على الأحبة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: After Abū Bakr died, Medina erupted in grief like it had at the Prophet's death; ʿAlī came weeping and said the caliphate of prophethood had ended.
rows.anchor: قال لما قبض أبو بكر رضي الله عنه ارتجت المدينة بالبكاء كيوم قبض النبي

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In his eulogy, ʿAlī praised Abū Bakr as the first Muslim, strongest in faith and certainty, most God-fearing, and foremost in service to Islam and the Messenger.
rows.anchor: كنت أول القوم إسلاما وأخلصهم إيمانا وأشدهم يقينا وأخوفهم لله

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī said Abū Bakr affirmed the Messenger when others rejected him, and that revelation named him among those who brought truth and believed it.
rows.anchor: صدقت رسول الله حين كذبه الناس فسماك في تنزيله صديقا

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī praised Abū Bakr's companionship in hardship and the cave, his succession to the Messenger, and his steadfast leadership when others faltered after the Prophet's death.
rows.anchor: ثاني اثنين وصاحبه في الغار والمنزل عليه السكينة والوقار ورفيقه في الهجرة وخليفته في دين الله

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: At the conquest of Mecca, the Prophet rejected tribal pride and status by ancestry, reminding Quraysh that all people descend from Adam and reciting that piety is the measure of honor with God.
rows.anchor: يا معشر قريش إن الله قد أذهب عنكم نخوة الجاهلية وتعظمها بالآباء

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: The Prophet declared former claims of vengeance, blood, or wealth void, except for custodianship of the Kaʿba and supplying water to pilgrims.
rows.anchor: ألا كل مأثرة أو دم أو مال يدعى - فهو تحت قدمي هاتين إلا سدانة البيت وسقاية الحاج

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: For a death caused by a whip or stick in an assault short of intentional killing, he prescribed an aggravated blood-money of forty pregnant camels.
rows.anchor: وقتيل الخطإ العمد بالسوط والعصا - فيه الدية مغلظة منها أربعون خلفة في بطونها أولادها

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: When the Prophet asked what he would do with Quraysh, they appealed to his generosity; he then released them, calling them free.
rows.anchor: قالوا خيرا أخ كريم وابن أخ كريم ثم قال فاذهبوا فأنتم الطلقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the poetic phrase 'you command the heart to act,' the verb means 'you command me'; Bāqillānī rejects the metaphor because a heart cannot be commanded.
rows.anchor: ثم قوله تأمري القلب يفعل معناه تأمريني والقلب لا يؤمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One gloss takes 'my garments' for the body, by analogy with the Qur'anic phrase about purifying one's garments.
rows.anchor: ذكر الثوب وأراد البدن مثل قول الله تعالى ( ﴿ وثيابك فطهر ﴾ )

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses the garment image as separation or abandonment and says tansal means to part.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة هذا مثل للهجر وتنسل تبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāqillānī calls the first line weak and low: its self-deprecating description would justify abandonment, yet the poet presents himself as refined and deserving continued attachment.
rows.anchor: وهو بيت قليل المعنى ركيكه ووضيعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second hemistich has an unusual but modest and intimate metaphor.
rows.anchor: والاستعارة في المصرع الثاني فيها تواضع وتقارب وإن كانت غريبة

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī explains 'aʿshār' as a heart broken into pieces, like a vessel called aʿshār when shattered; Bāqillānī considers this the more likely interpretation.
rows.anchor: هذا تأويل ذكره الأصمعي وهو أشبه عند أكثرهم

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the two eyes as the al-muʿallā and al-raqīb arrows, worth seven and three shares in the camel division, meaning she has taken his whole heart.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره وهذا مثل للأعشار التي تقسم الجزور عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrow reading avoids an awkward phrase but spoils the meaning: if the lover's whole heart already belongs to her, her weeping cannot make it wholly hers.
rows.anchor: ولكن من حمل على التأويل الثاني سلم من الخلل الواقع في اللفظ ولكنه يفسد المعنى ويختل
